Work in this order, one step per tool call:
1. Locate. Take the most specific identifier or error text from the issue and list the candidate files with one shell line through the run_command tool, for example `git grep -n "the_identifier" -- "*.py" | head -n 20`. If the first search returns nothing, search a shorter token; the file the fix touches is usually in the top few hits. Do not read files that are not in the hits.
2. Read only the function that must change, with the read_file tool and a line range (at most 150 lines). One or two reads are enough.
3. Edit the source with the run_command tool, one change per command, always in this form (the old block is a few lines copied exactly from what you read, the new block is their replacement; use r""" quotes instead if the code itself contains three single quotes):
```

<old lines, copied exactly>

If the command fails, read those lines again and retry with a shorter old block; never resend the identical command. Write a new file with `cat > path/to/new_file.py <<'EOF'`. Create new functions, parameters, messages or files with exactly the names the issue implies. Apply the same fix to an obvious sibling (both branches of a condition, load and loads) with one more edit.
4. Check. Run the one test file or test that covers this code, for example `python3 -m pytest tests/test_x.py -x -q -k name` with a 60-second timeout in the command, or run the issue's own example as `python3 - <<'EOF'` with an assert. Failures unrelated to your change are not yours to fix. Never run the whole test suite.
5. Submit. Call the submit_patch tool once the targeted check passes, or once you have made the best change you can and 20 tool calls or most of the time are spent. Then reply with one sentence and stop.

## Description

♻️ Validate Server Sent Event fields to avoid applications from sending broken data

This was reported multiple times as a "vulnerability" by users probably using automated AI tools, with the argument that if input was taken from the request and passed directly to an event unfiltered, it could break the client.

If an app sets an `id` or `event` with multi-line content, I would consider that app broken, and probably the app itself vulnerable to something, not FastAPI. With this change, if any app sets invalid multi-line values (sourced from unfiltered input or in any other way), FastAPI will make it a server error (which it is, as the app is sending invalid data).

I don't think the code before this PR has a bug, less a vulnerability. This change is mainly a quality of life improvement to prevent badly written apps from shooting themselves in the foot by passing unsanitized data directly to a SSE.

The `ServerSentEvent` class is a Pydantic model used to represent an SSE event.
The problem statement says that `id` and `event` fields should not contain multi-line content.
Multi-line content in SSE fields usually means they contain newline characters (`\n`).

The problem says: "If an app sets an `id` or `event` with multi-line content, I would consider that app broken... FastAPI will make it a server error".

```
